title: Iliad - Book I, The Wrath of Achilles
author: Homer
description: The opening of Homer's Iliad, announcing the theme of Achilles' wrath and its devastating consequences for the Greeks.

sections.greek:
Μῆνιν ἄειδε, θεά, Πηληϊάδεω Ἀχιλῆος
οὐλομένην, ἣ μυρί᾽ Ἀχαιοῖς ἄλγε᾽ ἔθηκε,
πολλὰς δ᾽ ἰφθίμους ψυχὰς Ἄϊδι προΐαψεν
ἡρώων, αὐτοὺς δὲ ἑλώρια τεῦχε κύνεσσιν
οἰωνοῖσί τε πᾶσι, Διὸς δ᾽ ἐτελείετο βουλή,
ἐξ οὗ δὴ τὰ πρῶτα διαστήτην ἐρίσαντε
Ἀτρεΐδης τε ἄναξ ἀνδρῶν καὶ δῖος Ἀχιλλεύς.
sections.translation: Sing, goddess, of the wrath of Peleus' son Achilles, the accursed wrath that brought countless sorrows upon the Achaeans, and hurled many mighty souls of heroes to Hades, and made them prey for dogs and all birds, and the will of Zeus was being fulfilled, from when first they parted in strife, Atreus' son, lord of men, and brilliant Achilles.

lineByLine.translation: Sing, goddess, of the wrath of Achilles, son of Peleus
lineByLine.notes: Μῆνιν: the first word sets the theme; Πηληϊάδεω: patronymic genitive

lineByLine.greek: οὐλομένην, ἣ μυρί᾽ Ἀχαιοῖς ἄλγε᾽ ἔθηκε
lineByLine.transliteration: oulomenēn, hē myri' Achaiois alge' ethēke
lineByLine.translation: the accursed [wrath], which brought countless sorrows upon the Achaeans

lineByLine.greek: πολλὰς δ᾽ ἰφθίμους ψυχὰς Ἄϊδι προΐαψεν
lineByLine.transliteration: pollas d' iphthimous psychas Aïdi proïapsen
lineByLine.translation: and hurled many mighty souls to Hades
lineByLine.notes: ἰφθίμους: 'mighty, strong'; Ἄϊδι: dative of Hades

lineByLine.greek: ἡρώων, αὐτοὺς δὲ ἑλώρια τεῦχε κύνεσσιν
lineByLine.transliteration: hērōōn, autous de helōria teukhe kynessin
lineByLine.translation: of heroes, and made them [their bodies] prey for dogs
lineByLine.notes: ἑλώρια: 'prey, spoil'; contrast ψυχάς (souls) with αὐτούς (bodies)

lineByLine.greek: οἰωνοῖσί τε πᾶσι, Διὸς δ᾽ ἐτελείετο βουλή
lineByLine.transliteration: oiōnoisi te pasi, Dios d' eteleïeto boulē
lineByLine.translation: and all birds, and the will of Zeus was being fulfilled
lineByLine.notes: βουλή: 'will, plan' - Zeus's larger purpose in the war

lineByLine.greek: ἐξ οὗ δὴ τὰ πρῶτα διαστήτην ἐρίσαντε
lineByLine.transliteration: ex hou dē ta prōta diastētēn erisante
lineByLine.translation: from when first they parted in strife
lineByLine.notes: διαστήτην: dual form - 'the two stood apart'

lineByLine.greek: Ἀτρεΐδης τε ἄναξ ἀνδρῶν καὶ δῖος Ἀχιλλεύς
lineByLine.transliteration: Atreidēs te anax andrōn kai dios Achilleus
lineByLine.translation: Atreus' son, lord of men, and brilliant Achilles
lineByLine.notes: ἄναξ ἀνδρῶν: formulaic epithet for Agamemnon; δῖος: 'divine, brilliant'

sections.greek:
Τίς τ᾽ ἄρ σφωε θεῶν ἔριδι ξυνέηκε μάχεσθαι;
Λητοῦς καὶ Διὸς υἱός· ὃ γὰρ βασιλῆϊ χολωθεὶς
νοῦσον ἀνὰ στρατὸν ὄρσε κακήν, ὀλέκοντο δὲ λαοί,
οὕνεκα τὸν Χρύσην ἠτίμασεν ἀρητῆρα
Ἀτρεΐδης.
sections.translation: Which of the gods then set these two to fight in strife? The son of Leto and Zeus; for he, angered at the king, stirred up an evil plague throughout the army, and the people were perishing, because the son of Atreus had dishonored the priest Chryses.

historicalContext: The Iliad, composed in the 8th century BCE, is the oldest work of Western literature. It depicts a few weeks during the tenth year of the Trojan War, focusing on Achilles' withdrawal from battle and its consequences.
literaryFeatures: In medias res: begins in the middle of the war
The contrast between souls (ψυχαί) and bodies reveals Greek views of death
